label: Spectral density and the periodogram — mastery test (unseen)

items.stem: For estimating the spectral density function of a time series, one can use:
items.explanation: The periodogram is the sample analogue of the spectral density — the squared modulus of the discrete Fourier transform of the data, equivalently the transform of the sample autocovariances. The other three are real tools for other jobs: the ACF describes lag structure, the PACF identifies AR order, and Yule–Walker estimates AR coefficients. This is June 2026 Q7.

items.stem: The spectral density function is the Fourier transform of the:
items.explanation: f(ω) = (1/2π)Σₖ γₖe^(−iωk), and inverting recovers the autocovariances — so the two descriptions carry exactly the same information. Because γₖ = γ₋ₖ the density is real and even, which is why plotting it on [0, π] loses nothing.

items.stem: The spectral density of a white noise process is:
items.explanation: Only γ₀ = σ² is non-zero, so the transform has a single term and f(ω) = σ²/(2π) at every frequency — 0.159155 when σ² = 1. Equal variance at every frequency is where the name 'white' comes from, by analogy with white light.

items.stem: ∫f(ω)dω over the full range (−π, π) equals:
items.explanation: Putting k = 0 in the inversion formula gives exactly the process variance. So the spectral density decomposes the variance across frequencies, and the area under it is that variance. It equals 1 only when the variance happens to be 1, which is why option A is a trap.

items.stem: For an AR(1) with φ = 0.8, the spectral density is largest at:
items.explanation: The denominator 1 − 2φcos ω + φ² = 1.64 − 1.6cos ω is smallest at ω = 0, where it is (1 − 0.8)² = 0.04. So f(0) = 3.9789 against f(π) = 0.0491, a ratio of 81. Positive autocorrelation means slow smooth movement, which is low-frequency behaviour.

items.stem: Bartlett, Tukey–Hanning and Parzen are names of:
items.explanation: They are the standard weighting schemes for smoothing a periodogram — equivalently lag windows, since weighting neighbouring frequencies corresponds to tapering the sample autocovariances. They differ in how sharply they cut off and therefore in how much they smear genuine peaks.

items.stem: The periodogram as an estimator of the spectral density is:
items.explanation: At a fixed frequency I(ω) is asymptotically f(ω)·χ²₂/2, so its mean tends to f(ω) but its variance tends to f(ω)², which does not involve n. Verified over 4,000 replications of white noise: the mean ran 0.156 to 0.162 against the true 0.159155 while the standard deviation stayed at 0.156 to 0.162 across n = 64 to 16,384.

items.stem: To obtain a consistent estimator of the spectral density one:
options: smooths the periodogram with a window
items.explanation: More data gives ordinates at more frequencies rather than better precision at any one, since each ordinate carries two degrees of freedom whatever n is. Averaging over m neighbouring ordinates reduces the standard deviation as 1/√m — verified as 0.152, 0.070, 0.035 and 0.018 at m = 1, 5, 21 and 81. Consistency requires m → ∞ with m/n → 0.

items.stem: For an MA(1) with θ = 0.7 and σ² = 1 under the convention yₜ = εₜ − θεₜ₋₁, the spectral density is proportional to:
items.explanation: |1 − θe^(−iω)|² = 1 + θ² − 2θcos ω = 1.49 − 1.4cos ω, giving 0.09 at ω = 0 and 2.89 at ω = π. Option B is what the PLUS convention yₜ = εₜ + θεₜ₋₁ would give, so the convention must be read from the question; option A has the AR form, with the polynomial in the denominator.

items.stem: The PACF is primarily used to:
options: identify the order of an AR process
items.explanation: The PACF cuts off after lag p for an AR(p), which is what identifies the order; the ACF cuts off after lag q for an MA(q). Neither estimates a spectrum — that is the periodogram's job, and offering both as distractors is exactly what June 2026's question did.

items.stem: The cumulative periodogram is used to test whether a series is:
items.explanation: Under white noise the spectral density is flat, so the cumulative sum of periodogram ordinates should rise linearly in frequency; the maximum departure from that line is compared with Kolmogorov–Smirnov-type bounds. It is the frequency-domain counterpart of the Ljung–Box test and is applied to residuals after fitting.

items.stem: For an AR(1) with φ = 0.5 and σ² = 1, f(0) and the total area under the density are:
items.explanation: The denominator at ω = 0 is (1 − 0.5)² = 0.25, so f(0) = 1/(2π × 0.25) = 0.6366, and the area must be γ₀ = σ²/(1 − φ²) = 1/0.75 = 1.3333. Option C is the φ = 0.8 case.
items.check: The area check is the standard safeguard: it must equal σ²/(1 − φ²), which is 1.3333 here, confirmed by Simpson integration.

items.stem: Consider the periodogram and its properties.
items.explanation: A is true, and it is why the estimator is inconsistent. B is true: the mean tends to f(ω). C is true and is the mechanism. D is false — more data improves resolution, not the precision at any single frequency.
statements: Var[I(ω)] tends to f(ω)², which does not depend on n.
E[I(ω)] tends to f(ω), so the periodogram is asymptotically unbiased.
Each periodogram ordinate carries about two degrees of freedom whatever n is.
Increasing n reduces the variance of the periodogram at a fixed frequency.

A.why: True. I(ω) is asymptotically f(ω)·χ²₂/2, whose variance is f(ω)². Verified: the standard deviation stayed near 0.16 for n from 64 to 16,384.

B.why: True — the mean tracks the true density, which is why the estimator is unbiased in the limit despite being useless on its own at one frequency.

C.why: True. The ordinate is built from a sine and a cosine coefficient at that frequency, and there are only ever two of them however long the series.

D.why: False, and it is the heart of the matter. Doubling n halves the spacing between Fourier frequencies, giving more ordinates rather than better ones. Smoothing is what converts that extra resolution into precision.

items.stem: A monthly series has an annual cycle. Its spectral density peaks at approximately:
items.explanation: A cycle of period p observations corresponds to ω = 2π/p, so an annual cycle in monthly data gives 2π/12 = π/6 ≈ 0.5236 radians per month. Option D is ω = π, the highest representable frequency, which corresponds to a period of 2 observations.
items.check: Frequencies lie in [0, π], so any answer above π is impossible — which rules out option B at once.

items.stem: An AR(1) with φ = −0.6 concentrates its variance at:
items.explanation: With φ negative the denominator 1 − 2φcos ω + φ² becomes 1.36 + 1.2cos ω, which is smallest at ω = π where cos ω = −1, giving 0.16. A negative coefficient makes the series tend to reverse sign each period, which is rapid alternation and therefore high-frequency.

items.stem: A smoothed spectral estimate's standard deviation falls as 1/√m in the band width m. To halve it, m must be multiplied by:
items.explanation: Halving a quantity proportional to 1/√m needs √m to double, so m must quadruple. The verification figures agree: the standard deviation fell from 0.152 at m = 1 to 0.070 at m = 5, slightly better than halved with m a little above 4.
items.check: Useful smoothing bands are therefore wide, which is precisely why the bias they introduce has to be taken seriously.

items.stem: Consider the bias–variance trade-off in smoothing a periodogram.
items.explanation: A is true, verified across m = 1 to 81. B is true: bias depends on the curvature of the true density. C is true and is the formal consistency requirement. D is false — selecting for smoothness selects for a wide window and therefore for maximum bias.
statements: Variance falls roughly as 1/m in the band width.
Bias grows with the window width and with the curvature of the true density.
Choosing the window width by how smooth the estimate looks is a sound procedure.

A.why: True. The standard deviation went 0.152, 0.070, 0.035, 0.018 at m = 1, 5, 21, 81 — tracking 1/√m closely.

B.why: True, which is why a flat spectrum suffers no bias at any width while a sharp peak suffers a great deal. The second derivative of a constant is zero.

C.why: True. The first condition kills the variance and the second kills the bias; both are needed, so no fixed band works for every sample size.

D.why: False. Smoothness is controlled by the window width, not by the data — any spectrum looks smooth with a wide enough band. Selecting for appearance therefore selects for maximum bias. The sound procedure is to examine several widths and keep features that persist.

items.stem: Why does the periodogram fail to become more precise as the sample grows?
options: the autocovariances are estimated with bias
each ordinate is built from two coefficients — a sine and a cosine — however long the series
items.explanation: At each Fourier frequency there are only ever two sample quantities available, so the ordinate behaves like a scaled χ²₂ with two degrees of freedom whatever n is. Doubling n halves the spacing between frequencies, giving more ordinates rather than better ones — extra resolution rather than extra precision. Smoothing is what converts the one into the other.

items.stem: For an MA(1) with θ = 0.7 and σ² = 1 under the minus convention, the area under the spectral density over (−π, π) is:
items.explanation: The density is (1.49 − 1.4cos ω)/(2π), and ∫cos ω dω over a full period is 0, so only the constant survives: (1/2π)(1.49)(2π) = 1.49. That equals γ₀ = σ²(1 + θ²) = 1.49 as it must. Options C and A are f(0) and f(π) up to the 2π factor.
items.check: Confirmed by Simpson integration as 1.4900. This area check is the quickest way to catch a lost factor of 2π.

items.stem: A sample ACF shows values near 0.08 at lags 7, 14 and 21, each inside the ±2/√n band, and the analyst concludes there is no weekly cycle. The best objection is:
options: the confidence band is computed wrongly
a cycle spreads its evidence across every multiple of lag 7, so lag-by-lag tests have little power; the spectrum pools it at one frequency
the ACF cannot detect cycles at all
more data would make each autocorrelation significant
items.explanation: Periodic structure distributes its signal across all harmonics of the period, so each individual autocorrelation carries only a fraction of it and falls inside the sampling band. The spectral density gathers those contributions at the single frequency 2π/7. The caveat is that one tall periodogram ordinate is not evidence either, since its standard deviation is about as large as the quantity it estimates — the peak counts only once it survives smoothing.
